survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The analyses use ICCS 2016’s complex two-stage stratified sampling design with schools as the primary sampling unit and intact classrooms sampled within schools. The book chapters state that all estimates incorporate the survey design, including variance estimation corrections for clustering (Taylor Series Linearization) and the use of survey weights that are rescaled so that all countries contribute equally to point estimates. For multilevel models (e.g., school effectiveness and corruption/tolerance models), survey weights are additionally scaled to the effective sample size and pseudo strata are included in estimation. The manuscript does not provide a single explicit weight variable name (e.g., W_FSTUWT), but it repeatedly indicates that survey weights from ICCS 2016 are applied and rescaled following established guidance for large-scale assessment secondary analysis.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The chapters use IRT-based scale scores and, in some chapters, WLE or IRT plausible values for civic knowledge and other cognitive measures; however, the text provided does not specify a concrete missing-data strategy (e.g., listwise deletion, multiple imputation) for item nonresponse or missing questionnaire/test responses. Because the dependent variables include IRT/WLE scores and some predictors are based on plausible values, missing-data handling is not described at the level of an explicit imputation/deletion rule in the excerpt. This represents a reporting gap for missing-data treatment in the secondary analysis pipeline.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The empirical chapters use ICCS 2016 grade 8 student responses from 24 participating countries/regions. The sampling frame is restricted to grade 8 students (average age 14) and uses the ICCS two-stage design: schools are selected with probability proportional to size within strata, then one intact classroom per selected school is randomly selected and all students in that classroom complete the ICCS instruments. For the citizenship-norm profile construction, the analysis uses 12 citizenship-norm items (Q23) and recodes the original four-point Likert responses into binary “important” vs “not important” before fitting a structurally homogeneous multigroup latent class model. For the school effectiveness and related regression chapters, the excerpt states that selected variables have less than 5% missing (mean 2%, SD 1%), but it does not specify additional exclusion rules beyond the use of the available ICCS sample for the specified countries.

data.outcome_summary: This book (and its included chapters) uses ICCS 2016 to study “good citizenship” as multidimensional and to derive person-centered citizenship norms profiles. The ICCS 2016 data come from a stratified two-stage probability sample of grade 8 students (average age 14), with schools as the primary sampling unit and intact classrooms sampled within schools; analyses incorporate the complex survey design via Taylor Series Linearization and rescaled survey weights so that countries contribute equally. Citizenship norms are operationalized using 12 ICCS items (Q23) and modeled with a structurally homogeneous multigroup latent class approach to produce five comparable profiles (comprehensive, socially engaged, duty-based, monitorial, anomic) across countries. Subsequent chapters use these profiles as outcomes or predictors in descriptive, multilevel, and regression frameworks, and they also include IRT-based civic knowledge and other IRT/WLE measures. The excerpt does not provide a single unified predictive ML pipeline; instead, it emphasizes measurement comparability and multilevel inference under the ICCS sampling design.
